fields.name: method
fields.description: When shown the demonstration, write 'hand_push' if the empty closed hand slides the cube on the table, 'tool_push' if the robot picks up the long bar and pushes the cube with it, or 'pick_place' if the cube is grasped, raised, transported, and released. Distinguish pushing from grasping by whether the cube rises with the hand, not by occlusion. On execution cycles copy the carried value unchanged. e.g. "tool_push"
fields.annotation: At the video cycle classify the demonstrated means of moving the cube: 'hand_push' when the closed empty hand slides the cube along the table, 'tool_push' when the robot first grasps the long bar and uses it to slide the cube, or 'pick_place' when it grasps and lifts the cube before transporting it. Keep this value throughout execution. Classify by actual object motion, not by whether the hand temporarily occludes the cube. e.g. "tool_push"

fields.name: initial_scene
fields.description: During the video cycle write 'unknown'. On the first execution cycle, when this field is 'unknown', write the current execution frame label. Otherwise copy the carried label unchanged. Use the retained scene rather than substituting the demonstration's object locations. e.g. "E0"
fields.annotation: At the video cycle write 'unknown'. At the first execution cycle write the label of its current frame, preserving the execution's initial cube position, cube orientation, target position, and bar geometry as one scene keyframe. Retain that label for the rest of execution, including when these features become occluded or move. e.g. "E0"

action:
On a video cycle output memory only. Execution starts with the open hand high above the table. Select the manipulation family from method; do not copy demonstration world positions. Use the initial execution scene, or the current scene when initial_scene is still unknown, to establish the original cube center C, target center T, cube yaw, and bar endpoints. Recover world coordinates using calibrated image rays and the table plane; account for cube height when locating its center rather than projecting the center of its visible silhouette onto the table. Use the wrist view to refine estimates. All distances below are metres. Let d=(T-C)/|T-C| in the horizontal plane. Use downward orientation, roll pi or -pi and pitch zero. Test arrival with tolerances appropriate to the reported pose, allowing approximately 0.015 horizontal error after a long approach; do not repeatedly reissue an approach just because the robot undershot it.

For hand_push: the initial waypoint is behind the cube at C-0.05d, z=0.02, closing the gripper at arrival. Set yaw along the push line modulo pi, choosing the equivalent angle closest to zero. This is a push with an empty closed gripper, not a cube grasp. When the closed hand is low behind the cube and the cube has not yet reached the target, move directly along the table to T-0.02d, z=0.02, keeping the gripper closed and preserving yaw. When that endpoint has been reached and the cube is on the target, open at the same nominal endpoint. Do not insert a lift or an intermediate overhead approach in this family.

For pick_place: with an open hand not yet over the cube, approach the original cube center at z=0.15, open, yaw aligned to a cube edge using the equivalent grasp orientation nearest zero. With the open hand above the cube, descend to C at z=0.02 and close. A low closed hand holding the cube near its original location must lift vertically to z=0.15; it must not immediately travel low toward the target. Use the retained cube center for this lift, refined by any small observed cube displacement during grasping. A raised closed hand holding the cube away from the target moves to T at z=0.15, closed, preserving its current orientation. A raised closed hand already over T descends to T at z=0.005 and opens at arrival. A low open hand at T after release retracts vertically to z=0.15, open. The visible held cube and finger separation distinguish a grasp from the empty closed hand used in pushing. Use current position relative to C and T, object attachment, and the motion frames to distinguish lifting at the source from lowering at the destination.

For tool_push: grasp near one end of the bar, leaving most of its length projecting from the hand. Identify the physical endpoint nearer the robot in world coordinates, not by image left or right. Define the horizontal grasp point G exactly 0.05 inward from that physical endpoint along the bar's reconstructed longitudinal centerline. Localize physical end-face centers, not silhouette corners. Fit a common bar segment and top-surface elevation to corresponding endpoints and longitudinal edges in the retained initial views and the current calibrated wrist view while the bar remains at its source. Intersect the visible top-surface rays with the fitted surface plane and take the midpoint across the width at each physical end to recover the horizontal centerline. Select the endpoint nearer the robot in world coordinates. Cross-check the reconstructed segment by reprojection into the available calibrated views before accepting G. Do not project elevated surface pixels onto the table or assume an unsupported fixed surface height. Refine localization consistently without changing this definition of G; the reached TCP is not a substitute for G. Initially approach G at z=0.20 with the gripper open and yaw along the bar's long axis modulo pi. Once the open hand is above G within the stated arrival tolerance, descend to G at z=0.01 and close. Do not substitute the measured, potentially undershooting TCP position for G or change the inward offset when the endpoint is observed again. Lift to G at z=0.20 only when the closed hand holds the bar low at its original grasp location after grasp descent. A low held bar that has already been transported behind the cube is not in this source-lift condition; recognize staging arrival before considering a source lift. Use the same geometrically defined G and preserve the bar-aligned grasp yaw throughout approach, grasp descent, and lift. When the held bar is raised and needs to be brought behind the cube, move to the push-start pose at z=0.02, closed. Apply the staging yaw resolution below only in this raised-bar condition. For this pose use the signed perpendicular n=(-dy,dx), where d=(dx,dy); do not substitute -n. Use this same signed n for both staging and the stroke endpoint. The intended contact region is about 0.10 along the bar from the grasp toward its long free end. Put the staging TCP at C-0.10d-0.10n, z=0.02, closed, with the long free end pointing along +n. Resolve its yaw from the directed attachment of the held bar: in the current raised-bar observation identify the horizontal unit vector u from the grasp toward the long free end, using the retained initial bar geometry to disambiguate the grasped end if necessary. With theta the current TCP yaw, command yaw wrap_to_pi(theta + atan2(ny,nx) - atan2(uy,ux)), where wrap_to_pi expresses the angle in [-pi,pi]. This rotates the long free end to point along +n while preserving its signed angular attachment to the hand. Do not reduce the staging yaw modulo pi: reversing an end-grasped bar changes which side of the hand carries its contact region. The modulo-pi choice applies only to the initial bar-aligned grasp orientation, which is preserved through grasp descent and lift. Preserve the resulting directed staging orientation throughout the pushing stroke. This puts the bar behind the cube with clearance before the pushing stroke. When the held bar is low behind the cube and the closed TCP is within approximately 0.015 horizontal distance of the staging position, prioritize the pushing stroke over both source lifting and restaging. Motion frames showing transport and descent of an already-held bar into this configuration support recognizing staging arrival. Do not lift again, repeat staging, or reverse the bar orientation because fresh localization differs slightly from the reached pose. Move straight along d to T-0.03d-0.10n, z=0.02, closed, preserving the established staging orientation. When the cube is on the target and the stroke endpoint has been reached, prioritize opening at that nominal endpoint over lifting, staging, or another stroke. Preserve the established staging orientation and apply the existing nonidentical-waypoint release rule. Do not mistake the raised bar at its original grasp location for completion of the push.

For any release that would otherwise command an identical current pose, retain the nominal endpoint if it differs by at least 0.002; otherwise add a 0.003 upward displacement while opening. Do not add a substantial retreat before release. Never use finger closure alone as evidence that the cube was grasped: inspect object attachment and method. If a situation is not covered, use current images and the retained initial scene to recover the closest unmet geometric condition for the selected family. If localization is temporarily impossible, use a short wait to obtain another observation rather than inventing coordinates or switching methods. If an action executed no steps, do not infer progress.
